prompt:
Role and task instructions:
You are a helpful, respectful and honest assistant.

User request:
[Goal] Practice playing the instrument.
[Condition] You are unable to read sheet music
[Initial plan] Choose an Instrument > Learn Basic Terminology > Start with Simple Songs > Experiment with Melodies > Stay Consistent
[Problem] You find the plan quite vague and miss necessary steps.

For a given goal, make the plan more comprehensive and concrete. For each step you plan to take, mark with '[Step xx]'.
answer:
[Step 01] Choose an instrument that fits your interest, budget, and available space. Borrow or rent one if possible, so you can try it before buying. Pick a beginner-friendly instrument or setup, such as a keyboard with labeled keys, a ukulele, or a guitar with a comfortable neck.

[Step 02] Gather what you need to practice: the instrument, a tuner if relevant, a metronome app, and a quiet place to sit. Set up a music stand or phone holder for lessons and chord diagrams. Tune the instrument before each session.

[Step 03] Learn how the instrument is laid out and how to hold or position it. Identify its basic parts, how to make a clear sound, and how to avoid strain. Use beginner videos or an instructor that demonstrates each movement.

[Step 04] Learn basic music terms through sound and diagrams rather than notation. Start with beat, tempo, rhythm, pitch, melody, chord, and bar. Clap along with a steady beat and count “1, 2, 3, 4” before trying to play.

[Step 05] Learn to read the visual tools used for your instrument, such as chord charts, tablature, numbered notes, or keyboard diagrams. Find a beginner resource that does not require sheet music. Practice matching one diagram to one note or chord on the instrument.

[Step 06] Choose one very simple song you already know by ear. Find a beginner tutorial or chord/tab guide for your instrument, ideally one that teaches only a few notes or chords. Check that the guide matches your instrument and tuning.

[Step 07] Break the song into short sections. First listen to the section, then practice its notes or chord shapes slowly. Repeat each section until you can play it several times without stopping, then join it to the next section.

[Step 08] Practice changing between the song’s notes or chords. Move between just two at first, keeping a steady beat. If the change is difficult, slow down, simplify the rhythm, and prioritize clean sounds over speed.

[Step 09] Use a metronome or backing track once you can play the notes reliably. Start well below the song’s normal speed and increase the tempo a little only after you can play the section accurately several times.

[Step 10] Experiment with making a short melody. Choose a small set of notes that sound pleasant together, play them in different orders, and record the results. Try changing the rhythm or ending on a different note.

[Step 11] Follow a repeatable practice routine: spend a few minutes warming up, review a skill you already know, work on one difficult section, then play something for fun. Practice for 10–20 minutes on most days, and stop if you feel pain.

[Step 12] Keep track of what you practiced and what still feels difficult. Record yourself once a week, compare it with earlier recordings, and choose one specific target for the next week, such as smoother chord changes or steadier timing.

[Step 13] After you can play the first song comfortably, learn another song using one new skill at a time. Revisit earlier songs regularly so you can hear your progress and build a small repertoire.
